cls: Antioxidant / dietary supplement - licensed drug for diabetic neuropathy in Europe (thioctic acid)
pharm: Naturally occurring sulfur-containing redox cofactor and potent biological antioxidant with insulin-sensitizing effects
quick: Diabetic neuropathy: 600 mg once daily orally (or 600 mg/day IV in Europe)
Take on an empty stomach (~30 min before food) for absorption
No established adjustment; caution in severe impairment
Limit; chronic alcohol/thiamine deficiency relevant in neuropathy
summary: Alpha-lipoic acid (thioctic acid) is a naturally occurring sulfur-containing antioxidant cofactor. In the US it is sold as a dietary supplement (not FDA-approved), while in Germany and parts of Europe it is a licensed prescription drug (e.g. Thioctacid) for symptomatic diabetic peripheral neuropathy, available in oral and intravenous forms. The trial-validated optimal dose for diabetic neuropathy is 600 mg once daily orally, or 600 mg/day IV for about 2-3 weeks; raising the dose to 1200 mg increases gastrointestinal side effects without added benefit. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach. It acts as a redox-active free-radical scavenger and metal chelator, regenerates other antioxidants, and improves nerve blood flow and insulin-stimulated glucose uptake. It can lower blood glucose (hypoglycemia, especially with antidiabetic drugs) and rarely causes insulin autoimmune syndrome, particularly in genetically susceptible (East Asian) individuals.
indications: Symptomatic diabetic peripheral (sensorimotor) polyneuropathy - main licensed indication in Germany/Europe
General antioxidant / oxidative-stress support (supplement use; no FDA-approved indication)

dosage.t: Once daily on an empty stomach
dosage.n: Optimal benefit/risk; 1200 mg/day adds GI side effects without clear added benefit

dosage.d: 600 mg intravenously once daily for about 2-3 weeks

admin: Take oral doses on an empty stomach, ideally about 30 minutes before a meal, to maximize absorption (food reduces peak by about 30%)
For diabetic neuropathy, the validated effective dose is 600 mg/day; higher doses add side effects, not benefit
Monitor blood glucose, especially in patients on insulin or sulfonylureas
Consider thiamine repletion in alcohol-related neuropathy
Use IV formulation only in appropriate clinical settings per European labeling
moa: Alpha-lipoic acid is reduced in vivo to dihydrolipoic acid; this redox couple scavenges reactive oxygen species, regenerates other antioxidants (vitamins C and E and glutathione, raising reduced glutathione levels) and chelates transition metals. In diabetic neuropathy it counters oxidative-stress pathways (increased polyol flux, nitric oxide inactivation and endoneurial microvascular damage), improving nerve blood flow and conduction. It also enhances insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, contributing to its glucose-lowering effect.

relative: Thiamine-deficient states (e.g. chronic alcoholism) unless thiamine is replaced
monitor: Thyroid status in patients on thyroid hormone

preg: There are insufficient human data on alpha-lipoic acid in pregnancy. Use is not recommended; avoid unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk.
lact: There are insufficient data on use during breastfeeding; it is not recommended.
renal: No established formal renal dose adjustment in standard sources; use with caution and follow product labeling, which may advise caution in severe renal impairment.
hepatic: No established dose adjustment; alpha-lipoic acid is generally well tolerated, but use caution in significant hepatic impairment given hepatic first-pass metabolism.

major: Antidiabetic agents (insulin, sulfonylureas and others) - additive blood-glucose lowering with hypoglycemia risk; may need dose reduction
moderate: Thyroid hormone (levothyroxine/T4) - may reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; monitor thyroid patients
Biotin - may compete for absorption (structural similarity)
minor: Chemotherapy with antioxidant concerns - theoretical interaction
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; food reduces peak concentration by about 30% and exposure by about 20%.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; chronic alcohol use depletes thiamine, and combined with alpha-lipoic acid may worsen neurological effects - consider thiamine repletion.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor blood glucose; alpha-lipoic acid can lower it.

common: Nausea, gastrointestinal upset, vomiting (dose-dependent, higher at 1200 mg)
rare: Insulin autoimmune syndrome (spontaneous hypoglycemia from insulin autoantibodies), notably in HLA-susceptible East Asian individuals

monitoring: Blood glucose, especially in diabetics on insulin or sulfonylureas
Thyroid function in patients on thyroid hormone
counsel: Take it on an empty stomach, about half an hour before eating, for best absorption
If you are diabetic, monitor your blood sugar - this supplement can lower it and you may need to adjust your diabetes medicines
Report shakiness, sweating, confusion or other signs of low blood sugar
For diabetic nerve pain, the studied dose is 600 mg a day; more is not better and causes more nausea
Tell your doctor about all supplements, including this one, especially before surgery
pk: Antioxidant effect rapid after absorption; neuropathy symptom benefit accrues over weeks
Short plasma residence; biological antioxidant effect outlasts plasma levels
Store at room temperature, protect from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved as a drug (US dietary supplement); a licensed prescription medicine (e.g. Thioctacid) for diabetic neuropathy in Germany/Europe
600 mg/day oral is the trial-validated optimal dose - 1200 mg adds GI side effects without added efficacy
Can cause hypoglycemia - counsel diabetics; antidiabetic doses may need reduction
Rare insulin autoimmune syndrome (spontaneous hypoglycemia with high insulin autoantibodies), more frequent in susceptible East Asian / HLA-DRB1*04:06 individuals
The R-enantiomer is the biologically active/natural form; commercial products are often racemic
missed: Take the missed dose when you remember if it is well before the next dose; if it is near the next dose, skip it - do not double up.
overdose: Case reports of large ingestions describe nausea and vomiting, severe hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, seizures and, rarely at very high doses, multi-organ toxicity. Manage supportively with glucose, correction of acidosis, seizure control and close monitoring.
